summary:
Costa Rica decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1971 and adopted marriage equality in 2020, the first Central American country to do so. The ILGA World Database records this alongside gender recognition and legal protections, and no current visa or entry rule targets LGBTQ travellers; in December 2018 the President signed executive decrees covering immigration rights for binational same-sex couples. A single 1990 instruction from the Minister of the Interior directing consulates to refuse visas to women travelling without a man is decades old and is not described as current policy.

Legal gender recognition is administrative. Executive Decree 41173-MP, in force since 2018, permits a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order; the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones operates the name change on official identification as a simple, free procedure, a route available since May 2018. The state health system funds gender-affirming care.

The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised Costa Rica's near-universal health coverage and specific protective legislation while recording concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups. She recommended intersectional data collection as a basis for policy and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

Sexual-orientation-motivated hate crimes carry enhanced penalties under amendments the Legislative Assembly adopted in 2020: up to 20 to 35 years' imprisonment for a hate crime under article 112 of the Penal Code, one to three years for exclusion or segregation under article 380, and three to ten years for inflicting physical or mental pain, intimidation, coercion or blackmail under article 386bis. The provisions as reported are framed around sexual orientation, and the inventory does not state whether gender identity operates as an aggravating motive under the same articles.

Detention carries documented risk for trans women. The Justice Ministry announced in June 2017 that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve a sentence in a men's or a women's facility, with relocation to the facility matching gender identity decided case-by-case and strictly voluntarily. Reporting in June 2019 nonetheless placed a trans woman, Stephanie, in CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility, where she said only two options existed; the Justice Ministry reported 23 transgender people in the national prison system at the time. She recounted identity-targeted abuse including a rape with a broomstick handle at La Reforma in Alajuela, witnessed by a custodian. The Supreme Court ruled in 2011 that same-sex couples have equal access to conjugal visits in prison.

The direction of travel is contested. A conversion-therapy bill has been stalled since its 2019 committee report, and in 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol.
